scope: Documented cases outside Africa where a government (national, state or municipal) or a government-contracted or government-sanctioned agency relocated, rehoused or placed displaced people (by flood, other disaster, eviction or deportation) into sites that were themselves flood-prone, and those sites then flooded or were officially or credibly assessed as flood-prone. Built for comparison with the eThekwini (Durban) Lamontville/Umlazi riverbank temporary camp (April 2022 flood-displaced; AG flagged 2022; flooded Feb 2025, 5 deaths).
method: Web search and fetch, September 2026. Each lead in the brief was searched; the primary or best secondary source was fetched where possible. Several sites (ReliefWeb, UNHCR, Inquirer, ScienceDirect, MDPI, Houston Chronicle) returned 403 errors; where a claim rests only on a search-engine excerpt and not on a fetched page, the notes say so and confidence is lowered. Quotes are verbatim from fetched pages unless marked '[search excerpt]'. No individual victims are named. Fields with no source support are marked 'not_found'. 'Alleged' marks claims made by litigants or advocates and not established by a court or official finding.

cases.place: Kannagi Nagar, Ezhil Nagar (Pallikaranai marsh) and Perumbakkam resettlement colonies, southern Chennai, Tamil Nadu
cases.relocation_year: Early 2000s onward; big waves after the 2004 tsunami and after the December 2015 floods (2015-2023)
cases.flooded_years: Perumbakkam: 2015, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2023 (per IRCDUC); Kannagi Nagar and Ezhil Nagar flood in routine monsoons, including 2015
cases.agency: Government of Tamil Nadu; Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board, now the Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board (TNUHDB), which built the tenements
cases.reason_for_relocation: Evictions of riverbank settlements (Cooum, Adyar, Buckingham Canal) presented as post-flood rehabilitation, flood mitigation and 'restoration of water bodies'. After the 2015 floods the Chief Minister ordered the resettlement of riverbank residents to the city outskirts.
cases.floodprone_evidence: The sites were built on the Pallikaranai marsh, floodplains and lake catchments (Thalambur and Perumbakkam lakes), which are part of historic flood pathways. A 2023 flood audit by the civil-society group IRCDUC documented repeated flooding.
cases.consequences: IRCDUC counts more than 23,000 families resettled since the 2004 tsunami and 2015 floods, 12,045 of them at Perumbakkam, and 83 settlements (about 19,817 families) evicted since 2015. Residents were marooned in the 2015 and 2023 (Cyclone Michaung) floods and relief was slow to reach them.
cases.deaths_at_site: not_found for these three colonies specifically (see IND-CHN-02 for Semmencheri)
cases.government_response: A draft Rehabilitation and Resettlement policy was released in October 2021 but had not been finalised when The News Minute reported. We found no official statement accepting that the site choice was a mistake.
cases.risk_known_before: Partly. It was widely known the land was marsh and lake catchment: Kannagi Nagar and Ezhil Nagar were built on the Pallikaranai marsh, a recognised wetland. We found no formal pre-relocation official risk assessment in the sources.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent tenements. People have stayed for decades (Kannagi Nagar since the early 2000s).
cases.distance_or_position: Former wetland/marsh; lake catchment; floodplain on the city's southern periphery, about 25-30 km from the original settlements
cases.blame_framing: not_found (no official quote). Advocates frame it as state policy: evictions 'under the guise of post-flood rehabilitation' (paraphrased in search summary of HLRN / Citizen Matters).
cases.resident_voice: A relief volunteer told The Caravan: 'People in Ezhilnagar were furious that not a single official from the government had come to visit them.'
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income, informal riverbank slum dwellers from inner Chennai. Down To Earth reports the affected communities are largely Dalit. Tamil-speaking.
cases.accountability_outcome: none found (no inquiry or compensation); the draft R&R policy remains unfinalised

quotes.text: faced flooding in the years 2015, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2023
Resettlement sites constructed by the Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board are located in or closer to ecologically sensitive areas
All of these resettlement colonies are sited on low-lying, flood-prone areas
Kannagi Nagar and Ezhilnagar are a huge problem, ecologically speaking. They were developed on a large tract of marshland

cases.notes: This is the closest structural match to Durban: people evicted from riverbanks 'for flood safety' were moved onto a wetland that floods. The primary report is IRCDUC's 'Resettled in the Paths of Floods' (OpenCity PDF).

cases.place: Semmencheri (Semmencherry) resettlement tenements, southern Chennai, Tamil Nadu
cases.relocation_year: About 2005-2006 onward (post-2004 tsunami and slum clearance); 6,734 apartments
cases.flooded_years: 2015 (16 November and 1 December), 2023 (Cyclone Michaung); residents describe five floods in eight years
cases.agency: Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board (now TNUHDB), Government of Tamil Nadu
cases.reason_for_relocation: Tsunami rehabilitation and clearance of inner-city slums
cases.floodprone_evidence: Low-lying marsh-edge land near Thazhambur lake. In November 2015 ground-floor homes filled with about four feet of water before dawn, and on 1 December the colony was cut off for days.
cases.consequences: Twelve deaths reported in Semmencheri in 2015. In 2023, six days without power, sewage overflow, no relief reaching inner streets.
cases.government_response: not_found (no official quote in the sources)
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent tenements; occupied for about 20 years
cases.distance_or_position: Low-lying land near Thazhambur lake on the southern periphery, about 30 km from central Chennai
cases.warning_at_site: not_found. The 2015 flood hit at about 3 am as homes 'rapidly' filled, which suggests no effective warning (inference, not stated).
cases.resident_voice: In 2023: 'Aren't we human? Didn't we cast our votes during the election? Why do they neglect us now?' and 'We were told that if they tried to reach us, their vehicles would've got stuck in the water.'
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income slum and tsunami-affected families, including fishing households. Tamil-speaking.

quotes.text: Twelve people are reported to have lost their lives in Semmencheri
Aren't we human? Didn't we cast our votes during the election? Why do they neglect us now?

cases.notes: Split from IND-CHN-01 because it has documented deaths. The death figure is 'reported', per The Caravan; we did not find an official death register for the site.

cases.place: Corail-Cesselesse relocation camp and surrounding Canaan area, north of Port-au-Prince
cases.relocation_year: 2010 (camp opened 22 March 2010; families moved from a Port-au-Prince IDP camp in April 2010)
cases.flooded_years: Assessed as flooding 'regularly at least once a year' (IOM, July 2010). Storms and wind damaged tents in July 2010; the camp was evacuated before Hurricane Tomas in November 2010.
cases.agency: Government of Haiti (site selection under strong pressure from the international community and U.S. military); camp built and run by World Vision, IOM and the American Refugee Committee
cases.reason_for_relocation: To move earthquake-displaced people out of overcrowded Port-au-Prince camps that were at acute risk of flooding
cases.floodprone_evidence: An IOM site report (29 July 2010), issued about three months after people arrived, found the site prone to floods and strong wind and said it should not be used for further relocation. A later MDPI study of the adjoining Onaville/Canaan area treats flood risk as a core problem.
cases.consequences: The camp grew from about 5,000 to about 10,000 residents, and the wider Canaan area to more than 100,000 people in informal settlement, with permanent erosion scars and flood-prone dirt roads. Shelters were built even after the IOM warning.
cases.government_response: UN-Habitat's director said the government, and President Préval, opposed the site but gave in to international pressure. World Vision said it had not seen the IOM report and did not consider the area high-risk (as reported by the Canada-Haiti Information Project).
cases.risk_known_before: Yes, before permanent build-out: IOM flagged it in writing on 29 July 2010, after the first relocations (March-April 2010) but before later shelter construction. It was not flagged before the first move.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Announced as a temporary planned relocation camp with 'transitional shelters'. It became a permanent informal city, still occupied more than a decade later.
cases.distance_or_position: Barren plain at the foot of hills, prone to sheet flooding and wind, about 15 km north of Port-au-Prince
cases.blame_framing: Blame was shifted between actors (government vs international community vs NGO). No one was found accepting responsibility. The former mayor said: 'local authorities were ignored and almost all the decisions were made by the central government… we were not at all implicated in the choice of the site.'
cases.warning_at_site: Before Hurricane Tomas (November 2010), a police officer at the camp shouted through a megaphone 'The hurricane is not a joke!' (search excerpt, Time). The language is not stated; Haitian Creole is likely but not confirmed.
cases.resident_voice: 'They just dumped us here'; 'Imagine: they put you here, but there's no work' (IPS, 2013).
cases.who_was_moved: Earthquake-displaced, very low-income, informal-camp residents from Port-au-Prince. Haitian Creole-speaking.

quotes.text: is prone to flood and strong wind. As reported earlier, it is flooded regularly at least once a year.
Due to the reoccurrence and magnitude of floods, this site should not be used for further relocation and resettlement of
Corail was created because of pressure from the international community. The government was opposed to it. Préval was opposed.
They just dumped us here

cases.notes: It is ironic that people moved away from flood-risk camps were placed on land later assessed as flooding annually. The IOM report itself was not retrieved; its wording comes via the Canada-Haiti Information Project and IPS.

cases.place: Bhasan Char island, Bay of Bengal (Noakhali district)
cases.relocation_year: December 2020 onward (nearly 20,000 by mid-2021; about 33,800 later reported)
cases.flooded_years: Signs of water on building balconies reported after Cyclone Amphan (May 2020). No catastrophic flood documented in the sources; the case rests on assessed risk.
cases.agency: Government of Bangladesh (Navy built the facility with Chinese contractor Sinohydro)
cases.reason_for_relocation: To ease 'severe overcrowding' in the Cox's Bazar refugee camps (government aim: 100,000 people)
cases.floodprone_evidence: The island formed from silt only in the last about 20 years and its shoreline keeps shifting. HRW says the embankments cannot withstand a category-three storm, and calls it a flood-prone island that could be submerged by a strong cyclone at high tide.
cases.consequences: HRW calls it 'an island jail'. It reports restrictions on movement and says ambulance boats cannot operate at the height of the monsoon.
cases.government_response: The government justified the move by camp congestion and pointed to the embankments and cement cyclone shelters it had built.
cases.risk_known_before: Yes. Rights groups and experts warned before and during the transfers (HRW 2019 and 2021 reports).
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Described by the government as a relocation facility pending repatriation to Myanmar; in practice long-term (years)
cases.distance_or_position: Low-lying silt island (char) in the Meghna estuary/Bay of Bengal, surrounded by an embankment, hours by boat from the mainland
cases.blame_framing: The government framed the move as a safety and congestion solution. No acceptance of risk was found.
cases.resident_voice: Refugees reported 'clear signs of water on the balconies' after Cyclone Amphan (HRW).
cases.who_was_moved: Stateless Rohingya refugees (Rohingya-language speakers), camp residents with no formal housing rights

quotes.text: Formed only in the last 20 years by silt deposit in the delta, its shape and shorelines have repeatedly shifted.
Current embankments around the island are inadequate to withstand a category three storm or worse.
a remote flood-prone silt island in the Bay of Bengal that is at risk of being completely submerged by a strong cyclone during high tide

cases.notes: The site has been credibly assessed as flood-prone, but we found no documented flood disaster there. Keep it in a separate 'assessed risk' tier from sites that actually flooded.

cases.place: Rohingya refugee camps (Kutupalong-Balukhali and others, 33 camps), Cox's Bazar
cases.relocation_year: 2017 (mass influx; land allocated by the government on deforested hills and low ground)
cases.agency: Government of Bangladesh (land allocation, shelter rules); camps managed with UNHCR and IOM
cases.reason_for_relocation: Housing about 930,000 refugees who fled Myanmar
cases.floodprone_evidence: Hilly, deforested terrain with flash-flood and landslide exposure. In the first 10 days of July 2019 IOM counted more than 400 landslides and at least 28 floods. The 2020 monsoon brought more than 600 landslides and more than 30 floods.
cases.consequences: July 2019: about 6,000 displaced and 2 killed. June 2024: 10 deaths (at least 7 of them refugees), 7,794 refugees affected and 1,191 shelters damaged. Repeated internal relocation of families from high-risk plots.
cases.deaths_at_site: 2 (July 2019, HRW); 10 including at least 7 refugees (June 2024, UN Bangladesh)
cases.government_response: Authorities allow shelters only of tarp, bamboo and similar materials 'to maintain the temporary character of the camp', and promoted Bhasan Char as the alternative (HRW).
cases.risk_known_before: Yes. Landslide and flood risk was assessed by agencies from 2018 (landslide risk studies; UNHCR/IOM relocation of at-risk families).
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Officially temporary; flimsy shelters are required by policy. Occupied since 2017 (9+ years).
cases.distance_or_position: Steep cut hillsides and low valleys/paddy land
cases.blame_framing: Monsoon and weather framing in UN releases. HRW places responsibility on the government's shelter restrictions.
cases.warning_at_site: not_found in fetched sources (a volunteer early-warning system exists in the camps but was not documented in these sources)
cases.resident_voice: 'Rainwater leaks in because there are now holes in the tarpaulin roof, and the storm can easily damage the shelters within seconds.' (HRW)

quotes.text: Refugee shelters are particularly susceptible to damage or destruction because the Bangladeshi authorities will only allow constructing them with tarp, twine, bamboo, or other flimsy materials to maintain the 'temporary' character of the camp.
tragic deaths of 10 people, including at least seven Rohingya refugees

cases.notes: The hazards are both landslides and floods. Like Durban, the 'temporary' label was used to justify flimsy shelter.

cases.place: Ashrayan-2 houses on Biramer Pachgachi Char, Sariakandi upazila, Bogura (Jamuna river)
cases.flooded_years: 2024 (houses lost to Jamuna erosion and floodwater by October 2024). The Ashrayan project generally reports stranding in floods.
cases.agency: Government of Bangladesh, Ashrayan-2 project (Prime Minister's Office; district and upazila administration)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Rehousing landless and homeless families, many already displaced by river erosion
cases.floodprone_evidence: The houses were built on an active river island (char). An architect notes that construction within 50 yards of a river is legally prohibited, yet Ashrayan houses were built along riverbanks in char areas. Officials had advised against permanent structures on chars.
cases.consequences: At least a dozen homes were lost to the Jamuna, 10 of them in one month, and residents dismantled others to salvage materials. Residents expected to move to yet another char, a second displacement.
cases.government_response: A local official asked about a separate Ashrayan site said: 'I have recently joined. The previous UNO worked on this project. I have no comment on it.'
cases.risk_known_before: Yes. According to The Daily Star, the relevant officials 'always advise the district administration not to construct any paved or semi-paved infrastructure in the char areas'; the 50-yard legal setback also existed.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Announced as permanent homes (semi-pucca). Some were lost within about 2-3 years.
cases.distance_or_position: On an eroding riverbank of an active char in the Jamuna; within the legal 50-yard setback
cases.blame_framing: River erosion and nature framing; officials deflected. No acceptance of responsibility was found.
cases.resident_voice: 'Now the houses given by the government are also going.' 'We have to leave this char again and take shelter in another char, as the river erosion is taking a dangerous turn.'
cases.who_was_moved: Landless, homeless and very poor rural char dwellers. Bangla-speaking.

quotes.text: In the last month, 10 homesteads under the Ashrayan project on the river island were lost in the river because of erosion.
Construction is legally prohibited within 50 yards of a river. However, these houses have been constructed along riverbanks in various char areas of the country.
Now the houses given by the government are also going.

cases.notes: The two outlets give slightly different house counts and years (69 homes built in 2021-22 per The Daily Star; 79 homes built in 2020-21 per TBS). Keep both and attribute each. The hazard is erosion plus flood.

cases.place: Kasiglahan Village (NHA resettlement), Barangay San Jose, Rodriguez (Montalban), Rizal
cases.relocation_year: 1999-2000 (Pasig River evictees); expanded after Ondoy in 2009-2010, including new units built on the flooded Phase 1K in 2010
cases.agency: National Housing Authority (NHA), with the developer New San Jose Builders
cases.reason_for_relocation: Clearing Pasig River banks and Metro Manila 'danger areas'; rehousing Ondoy flood victims
cases.floodprone_evidence: Former rice fields prone to seasonal flooding on the Montalban River floodplain. Water reached about 10 ft in Phase 1K during Ondoy. The local government declared the area a 'danger zone' in 2012, and flood simulations show depths above 5 m in parts of the site.
cases.consequences: About 4,000 homes flooded in 2009 and about 7,591 housing units affected in 2020. Residents waited on rooftops for rescue. The dike and riprap destroyed in 2020 were still unrepaired a year later.
cases.deaths_at_site: not_found (no site-specific toll found in the fetched sources)
cases.government_response: An NHA official cited budget limits ('P75,000 per housing unit'). The NHA and its developer kept building on the flooded phase in 2010.
cases.risk_known_before: Yes, before the later phases: Ondoy (2009) flooded the site before new units went up in 2010, and the LGU declared a danger zone in 2012, before Ulysses in 2020.
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent resettlement; occupied for about 25 years
cases.distance_or_position: Montalban River floodplain, former rice paddies, downstream of Wawa Dam; also near the Marikina fault
cases.blame_framing: The NHA cited budget constraints. Residents blamed dam releases made without warning. Activists (alleged) questioned the NHA-developer contracts.
cases.warning_at_site: No. Residents said the Wawa Dam released water without prior notice in 2009 (Bulatlat). The Montalban Relocatees Alliance demanded an early-warning system.
cases.resident_voice: 'The waters rose very quickly, unlike the ones before. We were not able to bring anything, not even extra clothes.' 'After Ulysses, people here get anxious every time it rains.'
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income informal settler families evicted from Metro Manila waterways and danger zones. Filipino/Tagalog-speaking.
cases.accountability_outcome: none found. Activists called for an investigation of the NHA and New San Jose Builders contracts (alleged irregularities, not established).

quotes.text: Around 7,591 housing units were affected during the flooding.
The waters rose very quickly, unlike the ones before. We were not able to bring anything, not even extra clothes.
We haven't experienced the big flood, but we fear for it to come every time there is news of big storm coming.

cases.notes: This is the strongest 'flooded, then rebuilt on the same ground' case. The academic paper 'From danger to death zones' (2026) is relevant but was not fetched (403); its title and summary come from a search excerpt.

cases.place: Tzu Chi Great Love Village (Tzu Chi Love City), Barangay Liloan, Ormoc City, Leyte
cases.agency: Tzu Chi Foundation (NGO) in partnership with Ormoc City government (land/beneficiary side) – the government role is not fully confirmed in fetched sources
cases.reason_for_relocation: Rehousing Yolanda survivors from destroyed coastal and informal areas
cases.floodprone_evidence: Per an Inquirer report (search excerpt), Block 20 is the lowest part of the resettlement area and floods in heavy rain. In 2025 water rose to about five feet (Tribune, search excerpt).
cases.consequences: January 2018: at least 1,172 people, mostly from Block 20, evacuated (about 300 families). September 2025: more than a thousand villagers evacuated and 1,185 families given relief.
cases.distance_or_position: Low-lying portion (Block 20) of an inland resettlement site
cases.who_was_moved: Low-income typhoon survivors, many from informal coastal settlements. Waray/Cebuano-speaking region.

quotes.text: [search excerpt] Block 20 at the Tzu Chi Love City, where the 1,565 families live, is the lowest portion of the resettlement area that is susceptible to floods during heavy rain

cases.notes: The Inquirer and Tribune pages could not be fetched (403); the details come from search excerpts. The builder was an NGO; how far government selected the site needs checking.

cases.place: Arbor Court Apartments, 802 Seminar, Greens Bayou, Houston, Texas
cases.relocation_year: HUD project-based Section 8 subsidies from 1991 (placement of low-income tenants, not disaster relocation)
cases.flooded_years: 2016 (Tax Day flood), 2017 (Hurricane Harvey); also reported earlier
cases.agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), subsidising a private owner
cases.reason_for_relocation: Placement of low-income households in federally subsidised housing
cases.floodprone_evidence: The complex sits in the Greens Bayou floodway. Per Houston Chronicle reporting (search excerpt), FEMA's 1985 map already put it in the 100-year floodplain, six years before HUD subsidies began. All 116 first-floor units flooded in 2016 and 2017.
cases.consequences: The complex fell vacant after Harvey. In 2018 tenants sued HUD, alleging racial discrimination and fair-housing violations. The City of Houston later blocked the owner from rebuilding, and the owner sued the city.
cases.government_response: HUD renewed its contract after both floods and declined to comment on the pending litigation (ABC13).
cases.risk_known_before: Yes. FEMA floodplain mapping (1985) preceded the 1991 HUD subsidies (per Houston Chronicle, search excerpt).
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent subsidised housing; tenants stayed for years
cases.distance_or_position: In the floodway of Greens Bayou (the complex backs onto the bayou)
cases.resident_voice: not_found (tenant lawsuit complaints about mould and flooding)
cases.who_was_moved: Very low-income, HUD-subsidised tenants. Texas Housers reports about 95% of residents are African American (complex-level statistic).
cases.accountability_outcome: Federal lawsuit against HUD (2018; alleged discrimination, outcome not found). The city's refusal of a rebuild permit was upheld by a judge, per a Houston Chronicle headline.

quotes.text: Literally half of the complex is within the floodway
The apartments are located in the floodway of Greens Bayou

cases.notes: This is government placement of poor households into a floodway, not post-disaster relocation. Per Houston Chronicle (search excerpt), 8 subsidised complexes in Houston were in the 100-year floodplain in 2016, and HUD had renewed most contracts after learning of the risk. Katrina evacuees in Houston flooded again in Harvey (Fast Company), but we could not tie them to Arbor Court.

cases.place: Omari returnee camp near the Torkham border reception centre, Nangarhar
cases.relocation_year: 2023-2024 (reception of returnees and deportees from Pakistan since September 2023)
cases.flooded_years: July 2024 (windstorm and flash floods); July 2026 (floods damaged the Zero Point returnee compound wall)
cases.agency: De facto authorities' Directorate of Refugees and Repatriation (compound); humanitarian partners (UN OCHA-coordinated)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Temporary reception of returnees, many forcibly deported from Pakistan (about 419,900 arrivals since September 2023)
cases.floodprone_evidence: Flash floods on 15-16 July 2024 destroyed 550 tents. OCHA notes that tents and mud huts in returnee areas are extremely vulnerable to flash floods.
cases.consequences: 550 tents destroyed; shower containers, latrines and solar lighting damaged
cases.distance_or_position: not_found (border valley; exact position vs drainage not stated)
cases.who_was_moved: Afghan returnees and deportees from Pakistan, often destitute. Pashto/Dari-speaking.

quotes.text: [search excerpt] The number of tents destroyed in the Omari camp near the reception center at the Torkham border crossing point increased from 400 to 550.

cases.notes: The OCHA page returned 403; the figures come from search excerpts of OCHA/ReliefWeb flash updates. This fits the 'eviction/deportation-displaced then flooded' category. We found no evidence that the site had been assessed as flood-prone beforehand.

cases.place: Relocation site in Kohod village, Tangerang regency (near the PIK2 development), Banten
cases.agency: Local government relocation linked to the PIK2 project (Agung Sedayu Group subsidiary developer). The government's precise role is unclear.
cases.reason_for_relocation: Clearing land for the PIK2 coastal development (a National Strategic Project)
cases.floodprone_evidence: Residents say the site was former rice field. It flooded to about 1 m depth in January 2025.
cases.government_response: The disaster management official said: 'Our mitigation in the field is to train … the community in case of flooding and provide education.' The public works official said: 'We found many water channels clogged with garbage.'
cases.distance_or_position: Former rice field in a low-lying coastal area
cases.blame_framing: Officials blamed garbage-clogged channels (implicitly residents) and proposed community training, not moving the site.
cases.resident_voice: 'This used to be rice field. Now it's a relocation site.' 'We don't mind having to be relocated, but please give us proper facilities that are safe and don't flood.'
cases.who_was_moved: Rural and peri-urban villagers displaced by a private-state development project; low-income

quotes.text: This used to be rice field. Now it's a relocation site.
We found many water channels clogged with garbage

cases.notes: Eviction-displaced people who then flooded. We need to confirm whether government or the developer chose the site. The Jakarta rusunawa lead (Kampung Pulo to Jatinegara Barat) did NOT show flooding; residents there report fewer floods.

cases.agency: Government of Sindh / relief camp administration (details not found)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Sheltering people displaced by the 2010 floods
cases.floodprone_evidence: Per an Oxfam figure (search excerpt of a ReliefWeb fact sheet), 37,000 people displaced in 2010 were still in Sindh relief camps when the 2011 floods struck, and many were displaced again.
cases.consequences: Many of the 37,000 people were displaced a second time (Oxfam via search excerpt). The 2011 floods affected 8.1 million people and killed 361 (NDMA).
cases.government_response: A ruling-party member said: 'We need tents, drinking water, water purification tablets, and medicines. Nothing we do is enough.' (CSMonitor, general flood response)
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Temporary relief camps, still occupied about 1 year later
cases.blame_framing: The researcher quoted by CSMonitor said the government 'failed to forecast the disaster despite their experience with last year's floods'.
cases.who_was_moved: Rural poor flood-displaced households, Sindhi-speaking region

quotes.text: failed to forecast the disaster despite their experience with last year's floods

cases.notes: The key 37,000 figure rests on a search excerpt; the ReliefWeb page returned 403. We could not confirm that the camp sites themselves flooded rather than people being displaced again more broadly. We found NO source showing post-2010 'model villages' in Sindh or Punjab were flooded in 2022; that lead was dropped.

cases.place: Kuttimale post-tsunami relocation settlement, Kalutara District
cases.flooded_years: not_found (site described as prone to flooding; sites 'normally flood during the rainy season')
cases.agency: Post-tsunami housing programme in Kalutara (IFRC/Red Cross-supported, with government-allocated relocation land)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Moving tsunami-affected families out of the coastal buffer zone
cases.floodprone_evidence: An IFRC evaluation (search excerpt) says Kuttimale (14 families) was built in an area prone to flooding and most plots needed earth-filling. Some sites were in areas that normally flood in the rainy season.
cases.risk_known_before: Yes (implied): earth-filling of plots shows the flood risk was known at construction
cases.who_was_moved: Tsunami-displaced coastal households (Sinhala-majority district; group not specified at site level)

quotes.text: [search excerpt] The settlement of Kuttimale (14 families) was constructed in an area prone to flooding, and earth-filling was carried out on the majority of the plots to raise them.

cases.notes: The PDF was downloaded but could not be parsed, so the quote is from a search excerpt. We found no flood event. Small scale.

cases.place: Temporary shelters (huntara) behind the Balaroa subdistrict office, Palu, and villages in Gumbasa, Sigi, Central Sulawesi
cases.relocation_year: 2018-2019 (after the 28 September 2018 earthquake, tsunami and liquefaction)
cases.agency: Government of Indonesia (huntara programme; Palu and Sigi local governments)
cases.reason_for_relocation: Temporary housing for earthquake and liquefaction survivors
cases.floodprone_evidence: Flooding hit shelter residents in April 2020. A Palu council deputy said the water surged from stone-mining areas and permanent-housing construction sites.
cases.consequences: About 20 families (64 people) displaced again in Sigi; a road, power lines and fields destroyed
cases.deaths_at_site: none reported at the time (CNN Indonesia, 29 April 2020)
cases.government_response: The Palu council deputy suspected inadequate environmental impact assessments (Amdal) for mining and shelter construction. The Sigi disaster chief said the flood was 'not as severe as the April 2019 flood'.
cases.risk_known_before: Partly: the area had already flooded in April 2019
cases.temporary_vs_permanent: Temporary shelters (huntara); many residents stayed 1.5+ years
cases.distance_or_position: Downslope of quarrying and construction sites
cases.blame_framing: Blamed mining and construction runoff and weak Amdal (environmental review); partly blamed on government projects
cases.who_was_moved: Earthquake and liquefaction survivors, low-income; Kaili-majority region (not specified at site level)

quotes.text: Air terlihat menerjang dari kawasan penambangan batu gajah dan pembangunan hunian tetap ke rumah warga (Water was seen surging from the boulder-mining area and the permanent-housing construction into residents' homes)

cases.notes: The flood was small, and the source does not say the displaced were deliberately placed on a known flood-prone site. Included as 'temporary shelter flooded'.

counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.lead: Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana, USA
counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.finding: Counter-example. The state (LOCD) bought 515 acres near Schriever, 6-12 ft above sea level, with lots planned 'well above the 500-year flood plain'. This is a relocation to higher ground.
FEMA screened sites against Special Flood Hazard Areas before placement. We found no evidence of trailers placed into flood zones.

counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.lead: Katrina FEMA group sites (Renaissance Village, Baker LA)
counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.finding: Well documented for formaldehyde and poor conditions, but we found no source showing the site was in a flood zone or flooded. Dropped.
The Military Road site is a former quarry that needed water-seepage mitigation. We found no evidence it is flood-prone or flooded. Dropped.

counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.lead: Roma relocations (Pata Rât, Cluj; Miercurea Ciuc, Romania; Serbia 2014)
counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.finding: Relocations went to a landfill (Pata Rât) and to a site behind a sewage plant (Miercurea Ciuc), which are toxic but not documented as flood-prone. In Serbia 2014, Roma settlements were destroyed by floods, but we found no relocation into a flood zone. Dropped.
The resettlement site was declared 'unfit for human habitation' (National Green Tribunal) because of pollution, not flooding. It is near the high-tide line, but we found no flood event. Dropped.
Resettled towns faced landslide and geological hazards that forced further moves, but these are not floods. Excluded from the flood cases.
The sites were chosen partly for their elevation. The flooding reports concern farmers left on marginal land, not the relocation sites. Dropped.

counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.lead: Honduras post-Mitch resettlements flooded by Eta/Iota 2020
counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.finding: UNHCR reports a Mitch-displaced community (Chamelecón area) flooded in 2020, but the source could not be fetched and it is unclear whether it was a government resettlement site. Needs follow-up.

counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.lead: Rio Grande do Sul 2024, Petrópolis, Puerto Rico, Iran 2019, Sendong (Philippines), Bulacan relocation sites
counterexamples_and_dropped_leads.finding: We found no sourced instance of relocation into a site that then flooded. Dropped pending more digging.

literature.citation: Double displacement – Interactions between resettlement, environmental change and migration. Geoforum (2021).
literature.key_claim: Resettled populations (Mt Elgon/Rwenzori, Uganda) face new environmental stress at resettlement sites and respond by returning to landslide- and flood-prone villages. Resettlement can produce a second displacement.

literature.key_claim: Families evicted for 'restoration of water bodies' were resettled onto historic flood pathways, and Perumbakkam flooded in 6 of 9 years (2015-2023).

literature.citation: The Caravan, 'Placing the Poor in the Flood Path: Post-Disaster Slum Resettlement in Chennai'.
literature.key_claim: 'All of these resettlement colonies are sited on low-lying, flood-prone areas.'

literature.key_claim: Post-2015 flood evictions were used to clear riverbanks, with resettlement to the flood-prone periphery.

literature.citation: 'From danger to death zones: Living with the floods in the resettlement site of Kasiglahan Village in the Philippines' (ScienceDirect, 2026).
literature.key_claim: An NHA resettlement site on former flood-prone rice fields repeatedly floods; the title frames resettlement sites as 'death zones' (not fetched; from search excerpt).

literature.key_claim: Asks whether post-disaster resettlement creates new risks (the title frames resettlement as potentially a 'risky strategy').

patterns_observed: Flood safety used to justify the move: people are evicted from riverbanks or 'danger zones' in the name of flood safety or 'water body restoration', then placed on wetland, paddy or floodplain on the urban edge (Chennai, Kasiglahan/Manila, Corail/Port-au-Prince). This mirrors Durban.

Cheap peripheral land is low land: sites are chosen because the land is available and state-owned. That land is often former marsh, rice paddy, river char or bayou floodway (Chennai, Kasiglahan, Kohod, Ashrayan, Arbor Court).

Warnings ignored or issued after the move: IOM warned about Corail within about 3 months, and building continued. Kasiglahan was rebuilt on the flooded phase months after Ondoy. Bangladesh built Ashrayan houses despite a legal 50-yard river setback and officials' advice against building on chars. HUD subsidised Arbor Court after FEMA had mapped it as floodplain.

'Temporary' becomes permanent: Corail, the Cox's Bazar camps, the Palu huntara and the Pakistan 2010 camps were all announced as temporary and lasted years. The temporary label also justified flimsy shelter (Cox's Bazar tarp rule).

Repeat displacement: the same households are displaced again by flood (Semmencheri 2015 then 2023; Kasiglahan 2009, 2012 and 2020; Sindh 2010 then 2011; Ashrayan char residents moving to 'another char').

Responsibility diffused: blame passes between central government, local government, international agencies, NGOs and contractors (Haiti). Otherwise officials cite budget limits (NHA), clogged drains or residents' garbage (Kohod), or the weather. We found no case where officials clearly accepted responsibility for choosing the site.
Weak accountability: the only litigation found is the Arbor Court tenant suit against HUD (USA). There were no inquiries, resignations or compensation in the Global South cases found.

Warnings seldom documented: early-warning failures appear as residents' complaints (a dam released without notice at Kasiglahan; a 3 am inundation at Semmencheri). Sources almost never record whether or in what language warnings reached relocated residents; this is a reporting gap to target.

Who is moved: low-income, informal or tenure-insecure groups, often minorities or marginalised at place level (Dalit-majority slum communities in Chennai per Down To Earth; stateless Rohingya; mostly African American HUD tenants at Arbor Court; landless char dwellers).
